Hey tell me what happened that day

June 8, 1967, the fourth day of the Six-Day War. The USS Liberty — a lightly armed Navy spy ship loaded with antennas and Hebrew linguists — was sitting in international waters about 13 miles off El Arish in the Sinai, monitoring the war.

Around 2 PM local, Israeli Mirage jets came in low and opened up: rockets, cannon fire, napalm across the deck. Then a second wave of jets. Then three Israeli torpedo boats closed in and launched torpedoes — one hit amidships, tore a 40-foot hole, killed 25 men in a single compartment. The whole thing ran about 75 minutes. When it was over: 34 Americans dead, 171 wounded. The crew somehow kept her afloat.

Israel's story, then and now: mistaken identity — they said they thought she was the Egyptian ship El Quseir, apologized, and eventually paid about $13 million total in compensation to the families, the wounded, and the U.S. government. Every official American inquiry backed the accident verdict.

The controversy never died, though. Survivors point out the ship was flying a huge American flag, had been overflown and identified by Israeli recon that same morning, and the attack was sustained and methodical — jamming her radios, hitting the life rafts. Critics (including Dean Rusk and some NSA people) argued Israel wanted the ship blind or gone before moving on the Golan Heights. Captain McGonagle got the Medal of Honor for keeping the ship alive — but it was presented quietly at the Navy Yard instead of the White House, which the crew read as the government burying the whole thing.
Does it make any sense that this ship could have been struck at all? Does it make sense it could have been struck in this wa?

As a legitimate strike? No. She was in international waters, flying a giant American flag, with a silhouette no Egyptian ship had — she looked like a porcupine made of antennas. There was nothing lawful to hit.

As an accident, the story needs a lot of simultaneous failures stacked up. The "we thought it was the El Quseir" claim is the weakest link: that was an Egyptian horse transport half her size, slower, and shaped nothing like her. Israeli recon had overflown the Liberty multiple times that morning and marked an American ship on their boards. And accidents are usually one bad pass — this was 75 minutes, multiple jet runs at close range, then torpedo boats close enough to read the hull number, plus life rafts machine-gunned in the water. You don't shoot a ship's life rafts by mistake; that's not misidentification, that's making sure nobody floats home.

The honest problem is the deliberate theories aren't clean either. A false flag to blame Egypt fails because they left 200 witnesses alive — you don't half-sink the ship if the plan needs it on the ocean floor. The "blinding" theory (Israel about to defy a U.S.-backed ceasefire and grab the Golan, and didn't want American ears on it) has the most internal logic, but it still requires believing Israel would gamble its entire American alliance on one ship staying quiet.

So: accident requires believing in the most incompetent 75 minutes in naval aviation history; deliberate requires believing in the most reckless gamble. Neither fits without forcing it — which is exactly why it's still argued about sixty years later.

Short answer: no, and that's the whole controversy.

The timeline: Eisenhower's people were already demanding AZC leaders register as foreign agents in the 50s. Then in November 1962, RFK's Justice Department formally ordered the AZC to register under FARA — because it was bankrolled by the Jewish Agency for Israel — and then later just... withdrew the demand.

Kenen had pulled the same maneuver personally back in '51: he went to the FARA office, was told to file as an agent of Israel, and instead wrote back saying he'd "severed relations" with the Israeli government — then kept lobbying, just reclassified as a domestic lobbyist. And six weeks after the '62 order landed, the lobbying arm incorporated as its own separate entity: AIPAC.

No administration since has forced the issue — Fulbright himself tried again in 1988 with a former CIA official and got nowhere. Meanwhile lobbyists openly working for other foreign governments register under FARA as a matter of routine. So whatever you think the right rule is, it hasn't been applied evenly.
